mainTopic: A worker eating his employer's crops: may he improve the fruit, and when does dipping in salt turn snacking into a fixed meal that needs מעשרות?
overview: The גמרא asks whether a פועל (worker) eating in the field may do things that improve the fruit itself, like singeing it. It first makes clear that the question is about preparing the fruit, not the worker's appetite. Two ברייתות that forbid singeing and similar preparations are pushed off: those bans could be about ביטול מלאכה (wasting work time). So the question is narrowed to a case where his wife and children do the preparing. A ברייתא that forbids dipping fruit in salt is also pushed off, because salt is like eating the fruit with another food. Next, another ברייתא that allows dipping in salt is set against that one. אביי answers by splitting ארץ ישראל from חוץ לארץ, but רבא rejects this. רבא rules that in every place, dipping one fruit at a time stays a snack, while dipping two makes a fixed meal that needs מעשרות, and he applies this to each kind of worker. רב מתנא gives a פסוק in מיכה as the source for the 'two' rule, and a new ברייתא about cows treading on grain begins.

steps.title: The question is about preparing the fruit, not the man
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off an earlier proof by saying it only dealt with preparing the worker to eat more. The real question is about improving the fruit itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: We never asked about getting the man ready to eat. Our question was about getting the produce ready to eat. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects an earlier proof by clarifying what its question really was. It is asking whether a worker may improve the fruit itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier source dealt with the worker preparing himself so he could eat more, and that is clearly allowed. The open question is different: may he do something to the fruit, like singeing it, so it tastes better? The earlier proof does not touch that, so the question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: we are asking / it is our question

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two kinds of preparing. Getting the worker's appetite ready is not in doubt. The doubt is only about doing things to the fruit itself.

phrases.english: About preparing the man
phrases.notes: He means things the worker does to himself so he can eat more.

phrases.english: we did not ask;
when we asked,
it was about preparing the produce. What is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought just before this section by narrowing the question.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The earlier proof, which was about preparing the worker himself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That proof addressed preparing the man, while the question is about preparing the fruit.

steps.title: Proof: workers may not singe grapes in fire
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says workers may eat grapes at the ends of their rows, as long as they do not singe them in fire. This looks like a proof that improving the fruit is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Workers may eat grapes at the ends of their rows, as long as they don't singe them in fire!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to answer the question. Singeing the grapes is forbidden, so improving the fruit seems to be forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Singeing is a clear example of making the fruit tastier. If the ברייתא forbids it, that would seem to answer the question: a worker may not improve the fruit.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Workers may eat grapes
at the ends of their rows,
provided that they do not singe them in fire!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: פּוֹעֲלִין אוֹכְלִין עֲנָבִים בְּרָאשֵׁי אוּמָּנִיּוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question as it was clarified in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker may not improve the fruit he eats.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא forbidding workers to singe grapes in fire.

steps.title: Rejected: the reason is wasting work time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that singeing was forbidden only because it wastes work time, not because improving the fruit is wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the reason is that he would be neglecting his work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof. The ban on singeing has a different reason: the worker would stop working to do it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making a fire and singeing grapes takes time away from the employer. That alone explains the ban, so the ברייתא tells us nothing about whether improving the fruit is allowed in itself.

phrases.english: There it is because of neglecting the work.

steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ban can be explained by lost work time instead of a ban on improving the fruit.

steps.title: Narrowing the question: his wife and children do the preparing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sharpens its question: what if no work time is lost because his wife and children prepare the fruit for him?
steps.simpleTranslation: When we asked, it was about a case where his wife and children are with him. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: Since lost work time explains the earlier ban, the גמרא narrows the question to a case with no lost work time. This sets up the search for a new proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If his family singes the fruit while he keeps working, the employer loses nothing. The only remaining issue is whether improving the fruit is allowed in itself.

keyTerms.meaning: in a case where there is

phrases.english: When we asked,
it was about where his wife and children are there. What is the law?
phrases.notes: They can do the singeing for him, so he never has to stop working.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לַן, הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refines the question so that the answer in step 3 no longer applies.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a worker may improve the fruit when no work time is lost.

steps.title: Proof: no singeing, roasting in the ground, or cracking on a rock
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא says a worker may not singe fruit in fire, heat it in the ground, or crack it on a rock. He may only crack it by hand, a little at a time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: He may not singe it in fire and eat, he may not heat it in the ground and eat, and he may not crack it on a rock and eat. But he may crack it by hand, bit by bit, and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא listing several ways of preparing fruit that a worker may not use. This looks like a proof that improving the fruit is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list forbids several kinds of preparation, and some of them seem to be about making the fruit tastier. That would suggest improving the fruit is forbidden, even with no family helping.

keyTerms.meaning: heat / ripen (by burying in hot ground)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
He may not singe it in fire and eat,
and he may not heat it in the ground and eat,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא יַפְרִיךְ עַל גַּבֵּי הַסֶּלַע וְיֹאכַל,
phrases.english: and he may not crack it on a rock and eat,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מְפָרֵיךְ עַל יָד עַל יָד וְאוֹכֵל.
phrases.english: but he may crack it by hand, little by little, and eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: לֹא יְהַבְהֵב בָּאוּר וְיֹאכַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries a new proof for the narrowed question.
steps.raayaObject: That improving the fruit is forbidden.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing forbidden ways of preparing fruit.

steps.title: Rejected again: wasting work time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the same answer: these bans are also because of lost work time.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, too, it is because of neglecting the work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the second proof the same way as the first. All these preparations take time away from work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Singeing, roasting in the ground, and cracking on a rock all mean stopping work. Cracking by hand, little by little, does not, so the whole list can be explained by lost work time. That means the ברייתא does not prove that improving the fruit is forbidden.

phrases.english: There it is because of neglecting the work.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 5 using the same reasoning as step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the list of forbidden preparations.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Lost work time explains the bans just as well.

steps.title: Support: a rock doesn't sweeten anything
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up its answer. Cracking fruit on a rock doesn't make it sweeter, so that ban must be about work time.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense. If you thought the reason was sweetening the fruit, what sweetening is there with a rock?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings logical support for the claim that the ban is about lost work time. The rock case seems to have nothing to do with taste.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fire and hot ground clearly change the taste of fruit, but a rock just cracks it open. If the rock is forbidden anyway, the common reason for the whole list must be lost work time.

keyTerms.meaning: it enters your mind / you might think

phrases.english: So too, it is logical,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ מִשּׁוּם מַתּוֹקֵי פֵּירָא –
phrases.english: because if you thought it was because of sweetening the produce,
with a rock, what sweetening of the produce is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection given in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That the bans are because of lost work time.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Cracking on a rock does not seem to sweeten the fruit, yet it is forbidden.

steps.title: Even a rock sweetens a little
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that cracking on a rock does sweeten the fruit a little, so the support does not prove anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: It's impossible that it doesn't sweeten it a little.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the support from step 7. Cracking on a rock also makes the fruit a bit sweeter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rock sweetens even slightly, it fits the sweetening reason too. So the rock case cannot prove the ban is only about work time. The rejection in step 6 still stands, but it lost its extra support.

phrases.english: It is impossible that it doesn't sweeten a little.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the support offered in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the support from the rock case, not the work-time explanation itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The claim that a rock adds no sweetness is wrong. It adds a little.

steps.title: Proof: workers may not dip fruit in salt
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says harvesting workers may eat without separating מעשרות, may not eat the fruit with their bread without permission, and may not dip it in salt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Workers who were picking figs, dates, grapes, or olives may eat, and they don't have to separate מעשרות, because the תורה gave them this right. They may not eat it with their bread unless the owner allows it. And he may not dip it in salt and eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא as proof. Dipping fruit in salt only makes it tastier, and it is forbidden, so improving the fruit seems to be forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dipping in salt barely takes any work time, so lost work time is a weaker explanation here. The ban seems aimed at making the fruit tastier, which would answer the question that improving the fruit is not allowed.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Workers who were picking figs,
or picking dates,
or harvesting grapes, or harvesting olives,
they may eat, and they are exempt,
phrases.notes: Exempt from separating מעשרות from what they eat.

phrases.english: because the Torah gave them the right.
They may not eat it with their bread,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נָטְלוּ רְשׁוּת מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת.
phrases.english: unless they got permission from the owner.
And he may not dip it in salt and eat!

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא will be the next test case. The גמרא now has to decide whether the salt ban is about taste or about something else.
steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: פּוֹעֲלִין שֶׁהָיוּ עוֹדְרִים בִּתְאֵנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier proofs were pushed off, the גמרא tries a new source.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker may not improve the fruit.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא forbidding workers to dip fruit in salt.

steps.title: Salt is a clear case of adding another food
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the salt ban. Salt counts as eating grapes together with another food, so it tells us nothing about the open question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Salt is certainly the same as eating grapes with something else.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from step 9. The salt ban does not settle the open question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dipping in salt clearly adds a second food, and that is plainly forbidden. The question being asked was about a case where nothing is added. So the salt ban cannot answer it, and the question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: something else, another food eaten together with the fruit

phrases.english: Salt is certainly
like grapes eaten with something else.
phrases.notes: Since salt is an added food, it is obviously forbidden. That is why it can't settle a case where nothing is added.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֶלַח וַדַּאי כַּעֲנָבִים וְדָבָר אַחֵר דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the salt ban in the ברייתא of step 9.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Salt adds a second food, which is clearly forbidden. The open case adds nothing, so the two cases are not alike.

steps.title: A second ברייתא allows dipping in salt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line 'he may not dip in salt' and sets it against another ברייתא. That ברייתא ends with 'he may dip in salt and eat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said: he may not dip in salt and eat. But another ברייתא says: if someone hires a worker to hoe and dig under olive trees, the worker may not eat. If he hired him to harvest grapes, harvest olives, or gather fruit, he may eat and does not need to separate מעשרות, because the תורה gave them this right. If he made a deal to eat one at a time, he may eat. Two at a time, he may not eat. And he may dip in salt and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that seems to contradict the salt ban from step 9. This ברייתא says the worker may dip in salt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא forbids the worker to dip fruit in salt. The new ברייתא lists the worker's eating rights and ends by allowing salt. For now it is unclear which worker that last line is about, and the next step works that out.

keyTerms.meaning: and they contrasted it, the opening for a contradiction between sources
to hoe or till the ground
he made a set deal with the owner ahead of time

phrases.english: And he may not dip in salt and eat.
phrases.notes: This is the line from the ברייתא in step 9.

phrases.english: And they contrasted it with this:
One who hires a worker
to hoe and dig around under the olive trees,
this worker may not eat.
If he hired him to harvest grapes,
hired him to harvest olives,
or hired him to gather fruit,
this worker may eat and is exempt,
phrases.notes: He is exempt from separating מעשרות from what he eats.

phrases.english: because the Torah gave them this right.
If he made a deal, eating one at a time, he may eat,
two at a time, he may not eat,
and he may dip in salt and eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the salt line from step 9 and opens a contradiction against it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in the ברייתא of step 9 that a worker may not dip fruit in salt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second ברייתא says the worker may dip in salt, which seems to clash directly with the first one.

steps.title: Which worker is allowed to use salt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which part of the ברייתא the salt line belongs to. It cannot be the worker with a deal, so it must be the worker who eats by תורה right, and that makes the contradiction real.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which part is this about? If you say it is about the last part, that is obvious: since he made a deal, he can eat any way he wants. So isn't it about the first part!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is sharpening the contradiction. It shows that the salt line must be about the worker who eats by תורה right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A worker who made a deal can eat however he likes, so allowing him salt would teach nothing new. That means the salt line must be about the worker who eats by the תורה's right. That is exactly the worker the first ברייתא forbade to use salt.

keyTerms.meaning: on which part is this said?
the last part of a source
the first part of a source

phrases.english: Which part is this about?
If you say it is about the last part,
since he made a deal,
he may eat any way he wants.
Rather, isn't it about the first part!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the contradiction raised in step 11 is real.
steps.kashyaTarget: The salt ban in the ברייתא of step 9, as it applies to a worker who eats by the תורה's right.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Permission to dip would teach nothing new for a worker with a deal, who may eat any way he wants. So 'וסופת במלח ויאכל' must refer to the רישא, the worker eating by תורה right, and that clashes directly with step 9.

steps.title: אביי: ארץ ישראל versus חוץ לארץ
steps.stepSummary: אביי says one ברייתא is about ארץ ישראל and the other is about חוץ לארץ. In ארץ ישראל, dipping in salt turns the eating into a fixed meal, and outside the land it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: There is no difficulty. Here it is talking about ארץ ישראל, and there it is talking about חוץ לארץ. In ארץ ישראל, dipping makes it a fixed meal. Outside the land, dipping does not make it a fixed meal.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי settles the contradiction by placing each ברייתא in a different location.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once eating counts as a fixed meal, the food needs מעשרות. In ארץ ישראל, dipping in salt makes it a fixed meal, so it is forbidden. Outside the land, dipping does not make it a fixed meal, so it is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult, there is no contradiction
makes it fixed, turns snacking into a set meal

phrases.english: Abaye said: It is not difficult.
Here it is in the Land of Israel,
there it is outside the Land.
In the Land, dipping makes it a fixed meal,
phrases.notes: A fixed meal is what makes the food need מעשרות.

phrases.english: outside the Land, dipping does not make it a fixed meal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לָא קַשְׁיָא. כָּאן – בָּאָרֶץ, כָּאן – בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction that steps 11 and 12 built up.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the two ברייתות into two different cases (two locations).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות give opposite rulings for the same worker.
steps.terutzMaskana: Forbidden in ארץ ישראל, where dipping makes a fixed meal. Allowed in חוץ לארץ, where it does not.

steps.title: רבא: Such a big gap between the two places makes no sense
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges אביי. Can something be a fixed meal by תורה law in ארץ ישראל and yet be fully allowed outside the land?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Is there anything where in ארץ ישראל dipping makes a fixed meal by תורה law, but outside the land dipping does not make a fixed meal, and it is even allowed from the start?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's answer. He finds it too strange that the same act would be completely allowed outside the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעשרות in חוץ לארץ are a rabbinic law, and rabbinic rules usually follow the pattern of תורה law. So if dipping makes a fixed meal in ארץ ישראל, it should do the same outside the land. רבא finds it hard to accept that it would be fully allowed there.

keyTerms.meaning: is there such a thing? (a challenging question)
from the start, allowed even before the fact

phrases.english: Rava said:
Is there anything
where in the Land, dipping makes a fixed meal by Torah law,
but outside the Land, dipping does not make a fixed meal,
and it is even allowed from the start?!

steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's split between ארץ ישראל and חוץ לארץ.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Rabbinic law outside the land should follow the pattern of תורה law, so an act that makes a fixed meal in ארץ ישראל cannot be completely allowed outside it.

steps.title: רבא's new rule: one fruit versus two
steps.stepSummary: רבא drops אביי's split between ארץ ישראל and חוץ לארץ. In both places, dipping one fruit in salt does not make a fixed meal, but dipping two does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: whether in ארץ ישראל or outside it, with one fruit, dipping in salt does not make it a fixed meal. With two, dipping in salt does make it a fixed meal.
steps.whatsHappening: Since אביי's answer was knocked down, רבא offers a different way to settle the two ברייתות about salt. He makes the difference depend on how many fruits are eaten at once, not on where.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי split the cases by place, and רבא just showed that this cannot work. Now the line is drawn by number. One fruit dipped in salt is still a snack, but two dipped together counts as a real, fixed meal. So the ברייתא that says 'he may dip' means one at a time, and the one that says 'he may not dip' means two at a time.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It drops the earlier answer and brings a new one.
Making it fixed, turning a snack into a set meal

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבא is saying salt never matters. Salt matters only when two fruits are eaten together. With a single fruit, salt changes nothing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the working rule for the rest of the section. Every case that follows is sorted by 'one at a time' versus 'two at a time.'

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
Whether in the Land or outside the Land,
with one, dipping in salt does not make it fixed,
phrases.notes: The word for 'one' here means one fruit at a time.

phrases.english: with two, dipping in salt does make it fixed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After challenging אביי in step 14, רבא replaces אביי's answer with his own.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the two ברייתות speak about different amounts eaten at once (one versus two), not different places.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought, like אביי, that the difference between the ברייתות depends on ארץ ישראל versus חוץ לארץ.
steps.terutzMaskana: In every place, salt with one fruit is still a snack, and salt with two fruits makes a fixed meal.

steps.title: Applying the rule to each kind of worker
steps.stepSummary: רבא applies his rule. A worker with a deal may eat only one at a time, salt or no salt. A worker without a deal who does not dip may eat two at a time. If he dips, he may eat only one at a time, even with the owner's permission, because the fruit has become טבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he made a deal: whether he dipped or not, he may eat one at a time but not two at a time. If he made no deal and did not dip, he may eat two at a time. If he dipped, he may eat one at a time but not two at a time, even if he got permission from the owner. That is because the fruit has become טבל for מעשר, since the dipping made it fixed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא now spells out what his rule means in practice for each kind of worker. The step ends with the reason: once the eating is fixed, the fruit needs מעשר taken off first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three cases. (1) The worker with a deal is treated more strictly, so he may eat only one at a time, with or without salt. (2) The worker with no deal and no salt may eat even two at a time. (3) The worker with no deal who dipped may eat only one at a time, because two dipped fruits make a fixed meal. In case 3, even the owner's permission does not help, because the problem is now about מעשר, not about the owner's rights.

keyTerms.meaning: He made a deal (agreed with the owner that he would eat)
One at a time / two at a time
It became טבל, meaning food you may not eat until מעשר is taken off

steps.confusionAlert: The owner's permission cannot fix the last case. The owner can give away his own fruit, but he cannot cancel the duty of מעשר once the eating has become a fixed meal.
steps.whatToRemember: No deal and no salt: two at a time is fine. Salt, or a deal: only one at a time. Two dipped fruits make the food טבל, and no permission helps.

phrases.aramaic: קָצַץ: בֵּין סָפַת וּבֵין לֹא סָפַת,
phrases.english: If he made a deal: whether he dipped or did not dip,
one at a time, he may eat,
two at a time, he may not eat.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא קָצַץ וְלֹא סָפַת – אוֹכֵל שְׁתַּיִם שְׁתַּיִם,
phrases.english: If he did not make a deal and did not dip, he may eat two at a time,
if he dipped: one at a time, he may eat,
two at a time, he may not eat,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּנָטַל רְשׁוּת מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת,
phrases.english: and even if he took permission from the homeowner,
because they have become טבל with regard to tithes,
and the dipping made it fixed.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָצַץ: בֵּין סָפַת וּבֵין לֹא סָפַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes רבא's rule from step 15 and applies it case by case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker with a deal eats only one at a time. A worker without a deal eats two at a time unless he dips. Two dipped fruits become טבל, so even the owner's permission does not allow them.

steps.title: What is the source that two make a fixed meal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that dipping two fruits at once makes the eating fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And that two, when dipped, make it fixed: from where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for the 'two' part of רבא's rule. This line sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number two looks like a random line to draw. The גמרא wants to know what tells us that two items together count as something fixed and serious.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?

phrases.english: And that with two, dipping makes it fixed:
from where do we know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the 'two' rule given in steps 15 and 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that two items eaten together count as fixed eating.

steps.title: רב מתנא's פסוק: gathered like sheaves
steps.stepSummary: רב מתנא brings a פסוק in מיכה that speaks of gathering 'them' like sheaves to the threshing floor. 'Them' means more than one, and gathering things together is like bringing in grain, which makes it fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מתנא said: as the פסוק says, 'For He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב מתנא answers the question with a פסוק. Gathering 'them', more than one, is compared to bringing sheaves to the threshing floor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bringing grain into the threshing floor is what makes produce 'finished' and ready for מעשר. The פסוק links that idea to gathering 'them', a group. So putting two together counts as gathering, and with salt the eating becomes fixed.

phrases.english: Rav Mattana said,
as the verse says:
"For He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor."

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק in מיכה compares gathering 'them' (more than one) to bringing sheaves to the threshing floor, which makes produce fixed.

steps.title: A new ברייתא: cows treading on grain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a new ברייתא about cows that tread on grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: cows that are treading on grain...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is opening a new ברייתא about animals working with grain. This is only the setup, and the rest of the ברייתא continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic moves from human workers eating fruit to animals working on produce. The case is cows treading on grain, and the ruling about them has not been given yet.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Cows that tread on grain,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the salt discussion is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not yet stated. The ברייתא only sets up the case of cows treading on grain.
